1.0.s.en: 1. The questioning of the prophet Habakkuk:

1.0.0.en: 1 The burden which Habakkuk the prophet did see. 2 O LORD, how long shall I call, and thou wilt not hear? I cry out unto thee of violence, and thou wilt not save! 3 Why dost thou shew me iniquity, and lookest upon wrong? for spoiling and violence are before me: and strife ariseth, and contention lifteth up itself. 4 Therefore the law is slacked, and judgment doth never go forth: for the wicked doth compass about the righteous; therefore wrong judgment proceedeth.

1.0.1.en: With boldness the prophet cries out to God, saying that he calls upon Him and He does not hear; he cries to Him again and again because of the injustice that prevails among the people, and He does not save the oppressed. So the people of God have turned into a hotbed of injustice, wrong, plunder and strife; there is no one who wants to listen to the Law, nor anyone who accepts a just judgment, but the wicked surround the righteous man to stifle his breath and bring forth judgment according to their own desire.

1.0.2.en: "How long, O LORD, shall I call, and thou wilt not hear?!

1.0.3.en: I cry out unto thee of violence, and thou wilt not save?!

1.0.4.en: Why dost thou shew me iniquity, and lookest upon wrong? for spoiling and violence are before me: and strife ariseth, and contention lifteth up itself?!

1.1.0.en: Therefore the law is slacked, and judgment doth never go forth: for the wicked doth compass about the righteous; therefore wrong judgment proceedeth" [2-4].

1.1.1.en: In a friendly reproach he says: "How long, O LORD, shall I call, and thou wilt not hear?!" For the prophet did not cease to call upon the Lord and cry out to Him, if not with the tongue then with the heart and tears, because of the bitterness of what the people had reached through the injustice of the wicked. He knocks at the doors of God's mercies with his tongue, his heart and his tears, mingling his tears with the tears of the oppressed and his sighs with theirs!

1.1.2.en: In every generation the children of God stand amazed at the success that the wicked oppressors seem to have, and they say with the prophet David, "I have seen the wicked in great power, and spreading himself like a green bay tree. Yet he passed away, and, lo, he was not: yea, I sought him, but he could not be found" (Ps 37:35-36). The bitterness of Jeremiah's soul, because of the corruption and injustice he saw in his people, reached the point that he said: "Oh that I had in the wilderness a lodging place of wayfaring men; that I might leave my people, and go from them!" (Jer 9:2), and yet Jeremiah, in his love for his people, did not leave them, in spite of the distress he suffered on every level.

1.2.0.en: We return to the words of the prophet Habakkuk to find in them a revelation of his person: he is a man of God who cannot bear injustice, and so he speaks with his God in an open dialogue without formality, officialdom, flattery or pretense, but speaks out of the unceasing groans of his heart and his tears that do not dry. This is the picture of the man of God, whether priest or of the people, whose prayers do not cease night and day, with the lips as with the heart and the deed... He cries out that God may remove corruption and injustice from fallen humanity, and so raise up every soul holy to Him. Therefore he asks and seeks and cries without ceasing and without despair, confident that God is able to act! The prophet also knew the secret of their evil, that it lies in the deviation from the divine commandment or the Law, for he says, "The law is slacked, and judgment doth never go forth: for the wicked doth compass about the righteous; therefore wrong judgment proceedeth" [4]. The Law, which sets the heart on fire and gives it life, becomes rigid and ineffective if the wicked surround the righteous man and corrupt his mind concerning the commandment.

1.2.1.en: If the men of God in every age cried out to the Lord because of what they saw of the wicked oppressors, who trifle with the earth, while the righteous live in distress and bitterness, yet because they laid their thoughts and hearts open before the Lord, they increased in honor in the eyes of God. But whoever looks at this state and yields to thoughts of doubt concerning God's care and His governance of the world, his soul is struck with sickness. As St. Augustine says: [Holy Scripture presents the thirty-seventh Psalm as a fitting remedy for the one whose soul is afflicted with this sickness. In brief, this Psalm affirms that the wicked live like grass on the margin of the surface; they appear successful in the winter of this world, but summer is coming and they dry up and burn, for they have no roots in the depths of the soil.]

1.3.0.en: 5 "Behold ye among the heathen, and regard, and wonder marvellously: for I will work a work in your days which ye will not believe, though it be told you. 6 For, lo, I raise up the Chaldeans, that bitter and impetuous nation, which shall march through the breadth of the earth, to possess the dwellingplaces that are not theirs. 7 They are terrible and dreadful: their judgment and their dignity shall proceed of themselves. 8 Their horses also are swifter than the leopards, and are more fierce than the evening wolves: and their horsemen shall spread themselves, and their horsemen shall come from far; they shall fly as the eagle that hasteth to eat. 9 They shall come all for violence: the look of their faces is forward, and they shall gather the captivity as the sand. 10 And they shall scoff at the kings, and the princes shall be a scorn unto them: they shall deride every strong hold; for they shall heap dust, and take it. 11 Then shall their spirit transgress, and they shall pass over, and offend. This their might is their god."

1.3.1.en: The Lord's answer to the prophet's question came thus: "Behold ye among the heathen, and regard, and wonder marvellously: for I will work a work in your days which ye will not believe, though it be told you. For, lo, I raise up the Chaldeans..." [5-6].

1.3.2.en: Truly, God keeps silent for a time, not ignoring what happens nor out of lack of concern on His part, but to give an opportunity for return without chastisement from Him; if man does not return from his evil, the Lord Himself undertakes the chastisement, using every means for edification.

1.3.3.en: A. God is working a work in their days which they would not believe if it were told them... He is long-suffering, but when He chastises He gives a profitable lesson, even if it is severe. As it is written in the Book of Deuteronomy: "Even all nations shall say, Wherefore hath the LORD done thus unto this land? what meaneth the heat of this great anger? Then men shall say, Because they have forsaken the covenant of the LORD God of their fathers" (Deut 29:24-25). And as St. John Chrysostom says: [God did not intend to punish so much as to reform them in the future... God is good and loving, not only when He grants gifts but also when He chastises us, for even His chastisements and punishments are of His goodness, and a great manifestation of His help to us]. He also says that if God drove Adam out of Paradise, it was in order that by his expulsion He might bring him back to Himself... So also, if God allowed the people to go into captivity, it was in order to awaken in them the longing for inner freedom and the yearning to return, not only to the earthly Jerusalem, but also to the heavenly one.

1.3.4.en: B. He says: "Behold, I raise up the Chaldeans," for He is the Lord of history and its director, who uses even the wicked to accomplish His good divine plan for humanity. The Chaldeans, in their love of plunder, took the people captive, but by divine permission for the repentance of the people, as though God raised up the Chaldeans specially for this work.

1.3.5.en: C. The Chaldeans point to the enemy of good, to whom we ourselves hand ourselves over as slaves because of our sins; the Lord protects us from him again and again so that we may not fall under his humiliation, but when we insist on submitting to him, the Lord leaves us under his hands for our chastisement. In this spirit St. Paul the Apostle asks the Corinthians to leave the young man who fell with his father's wife, delivered to Satan, to be delivered to chastisement, saying: "In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when ye are gathered together, and my spirit, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, to deliver such an one unto Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus" (1 Cor 5:4).

1.3.6.en: The traits of the nation of the Chaldeans here correspond to the traits of the enemy of good and his work against us:

1.4.0.en: The enemy of good is not an individual being but a nation, that is, a kingdom led by the devil as a king who has rulers, authorities and powers (Eph 6:12), who has his angels and his soldiers (Mt 25:41); and it is a bitter kingdom that offers out of its own what it has, namely bitterness, delighting and rejoicing in the misfortunes of others and their destruction; its goal is demolition, not edification.

1.5.0.en: The Chaldeans were an object of bitterness to all the nations around them; they knew neither gentleness nor covenants of peace, but only attack and fighting. In this they were an impetuous nation that swoops down on others to take them captive and humble them. So also the devil with all his angels storm the doors of man to enslave and humble him, to work on their behalf. They lie in wait for him, to storm in swiftly at the moments when the doors of the senses or the emotions open, and rush inside to proclaim their kingdom in them. Therefore the psalmist cries: "Set a watch, O LORD, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips," lest the enemy storm into his life.

1.6.s.en: Third: marching through the breadth of the earth:

1.6.0.en: The nation of the Chaldeans roamed in every place to seize peoples and kingdoms without hindrance, roaming as though over the whole earth to devour all, but it was not able to rise upward to humble those who had been lifted up from the earth. So the enemy of good sees that the whole earth has opened before him, and he walks in its breadth, so that he is called the prince of this world or its elements.

1.6.1.en: The limits of the enemy of good are "the breadth of the earth," for he is, as St. Jerome says: [like the serpent that crawls on the earth with its head and tail and the rest of its body, entirely clinging to the earth]. He devours dust, so whoever among us is earthly or of the dust becomes food for him, but whoever lifts his heart up to heaven to practice the heavenly life, without the love of earthly things pulling him down, the enemy cannot snare him!

1.7.s.en: Fourth: to possess dwelling places that are not theirs:

1.7.0.en: The Chaldeans encroached on the property of others and on their persons, reckoning that everything was theirs alone, that it was their right to plunder and possess without hindrance, so long as they had the power and authority. So the enemy of good plunders humanity, which is not the work of his hands nor his possession, but the possession of Him of whom "all things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made" (Jn 1:3). It is the nature of the enemy of good to plunder what belongs to God, in order to set up his dwelling and kingdom in the heart that He made to be His holy temple.

1.7.1.en: The prophet Jeremiah expressed this satanic trait in the proverb: "As the partridge sitteth on eggs, and hatcheth them not; so he that getteth riches, and not by right, shall leave them in the midst of his days, and at his end shall be a fool" (Jer 17:11). And Origen interprets this proverb, saying: [The partridge, known as a cunning bird, circles around the feet of the hunter so that he is occupied with her until she is assured that her young have escaped, and then she flies away, and the hunter takes neither the young nor their mother; in this she resembles Satan, who occupies man's mind with earthly things so that he obtains neither earthly nor heavenly things. This partridge often sits on eggs that are not hers, and when the eggs hatch the young stay with her until the original mother comes and gives a call that the young understand, and they leave the deceiving partridge and return to their mother. It is a living picture of what happened, for the devil embraced humanity as his young and seduced it with his deceptions, but in the midst of his days the Lord Christ came giving the voice of His love, declaring it practically on the Cross, drawing the deceived humanity to return to its true Creator, and the devil lost what he had acquired without right, and at the end of the ages he will be a fool, for he will perish utterly in the fires of Gehenna.]

1.7.2.en: Since the devil, like the Chaldeans, possessed dwelling places that were not his, or like the partridge that sat on what she did not hatch, he loses everything, even himself, through the Cross, which returned the believers to their Creator and Savior, and which condemned the devil and all his hosts, since He "took it out of the way, nailing it to the cross; and having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it" (Col 2:15).

1.8.0.en: The enemy of good is frightening and fearsome to the man stripped of defense, but the one hidden in Christ Jesus, who "went forth conquering, and to conquer" (Rev 6:2), the enemy cannot terrify him; rather he himself trembles before him. Let us hide in Him who alone is able to "enter into a strong man's house, and spoil his goods" (Mt 12:19). If the enemy is strong, the Lord has bound him with the Cross and drawn away from him his spoils, which are humanity, and the Lord Himself has become the commander of the spiritual battle. Fr. Theophan the Recluse says: [Know that our enemies and all their schemes are in the grip of our Lord Jesus Christ, our divine commander, for whose glory and greatness you fight. And since He leads you in the battle Himself, He certainly does not allow violence to be used against you, nor does He will you to be defeated by the enemy, unless you incline to their side by your own will].

1.9.s.en: Sixth: their judgment and their dignity proceed of themselves:

1.9.0.en: The nation of the Chaldeans is despotic in its opinion, subject to no law but its own whim, and the enemy of good in his dealing with us is governed by nothing but his whim, so discussion with him is of no use. Therefore the Fathers of the Church advise us not to give ear to his words nor to enter into dialogue with him, for his dialogue is full of deceit and is not constructive.

1.10.s.en: Seventh: their horses are swifter than the leopards:

1.10.0.en: In this chapter the divine inspiration gives us a living, realistic picture of the hideousness of the true enemy, the devil, who spends all his energies to enslave us:

1.10.1.en: In the speed of his movement in preying he is swifter than leopards, and in his cunning, working in darkness, he is fiercer than evening wolves; his sphere of work is without limits, spread in every place setting his nets; his capabilities are formidable; he is able to come from afar to pounce on his prey from where we do not expect; his ability to plunder and flee is like the eagle that snatches its prey and flies off with it; his constitution is the law of injustice, without mercy or understanding; in his nature he is a predatory beast whose face is forward like the beasts; his captives are like the sand, without number; he humbles the king and mocks the princes; his slain are mighty; he shatters strongholds and heaps them up as dust that he uses for the sake of his kingdom; he is wicked by nature.

1.10.2.en: And now we speak of these traits in some detail. As to the speed of his movement in preying, as we said, he is swifter than leopards. He is swift in movement, full of craftiness and cunning, seizing every opportunity to hunt the soul, watching for the least negligence or slackness to draw the soul into his net. The believers, for their part, are watchful, seizing every opportunity to grow and to enjoy the crown... The spiritual life in truth is seizing opportunities: the enemy seizes the opportunity, and the believer seizes the opportunity. It is a continual spiritual struggle for each to reach his goal. We can sense this from the words of St. Ignatius of Antioch, who hastened to write to the Romans to stop the plan they had made to rescue him from martyrdom, since he counted that as love, but untimely... He counted his martyrdom an opportunity that might not be repeated, so why should they deprive him of it?! He says: [I beg you not to show me kindness out of season, but allow me to be food for the wild beasts, through whom it is granted me to attain to God. I am the bread of God; let me be ground by the teeth of the wild beasts, that they may become my tomb, and leave nothing of my body, so that when I die I may be a burden to no one... Entreat Christ for me that by these means I may be found a sacrifice to God... May I have joy of the wild beasts that are prepared for me, and I pray that they may be found eager to rush upon me, and I will entice them to devour me quickly].

1.11.s.en: Eighth: fiercer than the evening wolves:

1.11.0.en: If the devil moves by day like a leopard with great lightness together with cunning, in the evening he does not stop but goes out like evening wolves to seize. He knows no rest by day nor by night, so it behooves us to persevere without ceasing... even in the moments of sleep our souls say, "I sleep, but my heart waketh" (Song 5:2).

1.11.1.en: Fr. Theophan the Recluse sees that the believer not only perseveres, guarded against the blows of Satan, but by the power of the Spirit stirs up war against him to seize from him every position he had previously occupied inside the heart, saying: [If you wish, my brother, to gain a swift and easy victory over your enemies, you must wage war without ceasing and courageously against all your passions... Therefore our spiritual warfare must be continual without ceasing, supported by watchfulness and courage of soul, and these can be reached easily if you ask for them as a gift from God. So continue in the battle without hesitation].

1.11.2.en: Like the evening wolves he works in darkness to hide his tricks and schemes (Eph 6:11). As St. John Chrysostom says: [This enemy fights us not in an open and clear way but by schemes... He does not propose sins to us in their true colors... but presents them in another garment, to make his speech acceptable and disguised].

1.12.s.en: Ninth: their horsemen spread themselves, they come from far:

1.12.0.en: The enemy of good sets his snares in every place, spending all his energies to hunt souls even if the person is in a holy place. He dared to fight the Lord Christ on the pinnacle of the temple, and the Lord permitted him this in order to warn us, assuring us that the enemy fights in every place, at home as at work, in the church as in the street, in the closet where private prayer is made and during communal worship. Wherever he finds us he creeps toward us, in the hope of finding a place in our hearts.

1.12.1.en: As for his coming from afar, it means that he fights us from where we do not expect. Therefore it behooves us to have a burning spiritual insight that understands the mysteries of spiritual warfare and knows the tricks and deceptions of the devil.

1.13.s.en: Tenth: their horsemen fly as the eagle that hasteth to eat:

1.13.0.en: Origen says: [The eagle can see its prey from a great height, and with snatching speed it swoops on it and flies off, and no one can pull it from its claws. So the horsemen of the devil, or his demons, watch the soul to know when to swoop on it with extreme speed, and through the astounding surprise man descends into sin in a short time to find that he has lost much. If building needs a long time, demolition takes place in simple moments, and if the holy virtues require long striving in the Lord, their demolition is accomplished in simple moments of negligence]. And as St. John Chrysostom says: [A swift blow of the sword, lasting only moments, wounds a man so that he is treated for it perhaps for years, and it may end his life. So the enemy strikes with his sword in our moments of negligence... but these moments spoil the striving of long years!].

1.14.s.en: Eleventh: they come all for violence [9]:

1.14.0.en: The law of the devil, or the constitution by which he works, is the "law of injustice"; he seeks only to deprive us of the greatest good, and to draw us away from the heavenly life, that we may not be bound to the divine law or the truth. St. John Chrysostom says of the demons: [They do not wrestle to gain anything, but to corrupt us... Satan spends all his energy to drive us out of heaven].

1.15.s.en: Twelfth: the look of their faces is forward:

1.15.0.en: Perhaps by this he means that they are not like human beings, who have the lifted face that seeks heaven, but have the trait of predatory beasts that stretch out their faces to prey without tenderness or pity!

1.16.s.en: Thirteenth: they gather captives as the sand:

1.16.0.en: The devil hunts souls without number and takes them captive like sand, for he has been titled "the prince of this world" and "the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now worketh in the children of disobedience" (Eph 2:2). St. John Chrysostom says: [Why does (the Apostle) call Satan the prince of the world? Because nearly all humanity has gathered around him, and they have become slaves to him by their own will and free choice].

1.17.s.en: Fourteenth: they scoff at the kings, and the princes are a scorn unto them [10]:

1.17.0.en: Every time the people fell into captivity, the king was humbled and the great ones became an object of mockery and ridicule before the victors; when Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem and the cities of Judah captive, he ordered the sons of King Zedekiah slain before his eyes, and put out the king's eyes and carried him to Babylon to mock him. So when a believer falls under the hands of the enemy of good because of his carelessness or slackness, he mocks him.

1.17.1.en: If we in Christ Jesus, the King of kings, have become spiritual kings (Rev 1:6; 5:10), the devil spends all his energies to take us captive, despising us.

1.17.2.en: In our study of the Book of Hosea we saw that the king points to the human will, which reigns over man to manage all his affairs, and the princes point to man's energies and gifts... For when the enemy takes a person captive, he mocks his human will, depriving him of it so that he lives the rest of his life as a humble slave doing the will of his new master (Satan), and he squanders his gifts and energies (the princes) to make of them a mockery and ridicule! The enemy of good makes man lose everything: his will, his gifts, his energies, even his body also, and finally carries him with him to where there is perpetual perdition.

1.18.0.en: Strongholds could not stand before the nation of the Chaldeans, and so also no one can fortify himself, neither by his long experience, nor by his abilities and gifts, nor by rationalistic intellectual knowledge, nor by his dignity or the kind of his work... When the devil laughs at these strongholds, one stronghold remains which, if we cling to it, he cannot approach, namely the Lord Christ, the Rock of ages.

1.18.1.en: St. Jerome says: [The Lord Christ is the smooth Rock (1 Cor 10:4) on which the serpent cannot crawl, so whoever fortifies himself in Him is protected from the enemy, the old serpent].

1.19.s.en: Sixteenth: they heap dust, and take it:

1.19.0.en: In further humiliation the enemy demolishes the lofty stronghold and turns it into dust, then the enemy returns and uses the dust for the sake of his kingdom, that is, for his benefit. I say this is a bitter picture of the devil's work in the lives of those taken captive by him: he turns their lives into dust, drawing their hearts to the earth and corrupting their nature... and then he uses this dust as earthen vessels bearing his traits to hunt others.

1.19.1.en: Although the enemy fell from heaven, he does not cease to spend all his energies, not only to deprive his victim of the heavenly life and bring him down to the love of earthly things, but he also uses him to bring others down and deprive them of the heavens that are within them.

1.20.s.en: Seventeenth: their spirit transgresses and passes over; this their might is their god [11]:

1.20.0.en: Their spirit transgresses or changes to what is worse or more wicked, passing from evil to evil, and from iniquity to iniquity... looking to their iniquity and plunder as the might of their god who gives them victory over the peoples. They reckoned that their gods were stronger than the God of Israel, so they clung all the more to their idolatry and boasted in it.

1.21.s.en: 3. Habakkuk has compassion on his people

1.21.0.en: 12 Art thou not from everlasting, O LORD my God, mine Holy One? We shall not die. O LORD, thou hast ordained them for judgment; and, O Rock, thou hast established them for correction. 13 Thou art of purer eyes than to behold evil, and canst not look on iniquity: wherefore lookest thou upon the plunderers, and holdest thy peace when the wicked devoureth the man that is more righteous than he? 14 And makest men as the fishes of the sea, as the creeping things, that have no ruler over them? 15 They take up all of them with the angle, they catch them in their net, and gather them in their drag: therefore they rejoice and are glad. 16 Therefore they sacrifice unto their net, and burn incense unto their drag; because by them their portion is fat, and their meat plenteous. 17 Shall they therefore empty their net, and not spare continually to slay the nations?

1.21.1.en: The prophet Habakkuk, filled with zeal for the glory of God, so that he cried out and groaned, asking why God keeps silent about the wicked surrounding the righteous, corrupting his mind and his life, sees by the spirit of prophecy the fall of the Jewish people, marked at that time by injustice, falling under the bitter slavery of the Chaldeans, and he could not bear it. And as much as the prophet was marked by the openness of his heart toward God, speaking to Him frankly and boldly without formality or pretense, he was also marked by love for his people, so that he could not bear to see them suffering at the hands of a wicked and cruel nation, even if this was by divine permission for chastisement. He cannot bear the groans of his brethren and their bitterness, as though he says with the prophet Jeremiah: "For the hurt of the daughter of my people am I hurt; I mourn; astonishment hath taken hold on me" (Jer 8:21).

1.21.2.en: Truly, it is God who allows the chastisement of His children for their sins, but while He chastises, He does not accept that anyone should gloat over them, but requires us to groan with their groans and cry for their pains and be broken with their brokenness. God chastised Judah by the Babylonian captivity, and when the sons of Edom stood gloating, He rebuked them, saying: "But thou shouldest not have looked on the day of thy brother in the day of his calamity; neither shouldest thou have rejoiced over the children of Judah in the day of their destruction; neither shouldest thou have spoken proudly in the day of distress" (Obad 12).

1.21.3.en: As Habakkuk has compassion on his people fallen under the yoke of the Chaldeans, he reproaches God, saying: "Art thou not from everlasting, O LORD my God, mine Holy One?!" [12]. As though he says: How do You bear, O Lord, to see the Chaldeans, the wicked nation, plunder Your people and wrong them while You keep silent, though You are the Holy One who cannot bear evil?! You are my God, committed to my peace and security, not only for myself but for the whole people also. If You are my God who cares for me, will You not care for Your people?!

1.21.4.en: How beautiful are the prophet's feelings: in moments of bitter reproach he calls the Lord "my God, my Holy One," as though in his soul's distress he finds the Lord clinging to him, caring for him and embracing him as belonging to Him, for He is his own God and his own Holy One!

1.21.5.en: Let us reproach the Lord with all bitterness, but in our reproach let us see His clinging to us and His claiming us as His own, so that we cling all the more to Him and throw ourselves into His embrace, believing in His work with us and in us.

1.21.6.en: When our heart opens in love toward others and we intercede for them or ask on their behalf, the Lord becomes ours, for He clings to those who love and glories in His children whose hearts are enlarged!

1.21.7.en: The prophet continues his reproach, saying: "We shall not die. O LORD, thou hast ordained them for judgment; and, O Rock, thou hast established them for correction" [12].

1.21.8.en: The prophet says: "We shall not die," for he realized that the Lord, his God and his everlasting Holy One, in His love for His people pours His traits upon them, for since He is everlasting, above the limits of time, He gives His children "immortality"; they shall not die... Though in their evil they deserve death, in the living Lord they live. The Lord God says: "Because I live, ye shall live also" (Jn 14:19). He delivered them to the Chaldeans for chastisement, but as the psalmist says: "The LORD hath chastened me sore: but he hath not given me over unto death" (Ps 118:18).

1.21.9.en: God gave the Chaldeans the authority to chastise the people, and "to take the spoil, and to take the prey" (Isa 10:6), but not unlimited authority, but to the extent that God sees the salvation of His people in it, so the prophet says: "O LORD, thou hast ordained them for judgment; and, O Rock, thou hast established them for correction." So the limit of authority is that their work and plunder be for chastisement and judgment and not for destruction. Therefore when Satan asked the Lord to allow him to trouble Job, the Lord answered him: "Behold, he is in thine hand; but save his life" (Job 2:7). The Lord says to the sea: "Hitherto shalt thou come, but no further: and here shall thy proud waves be stayed" (Job 38:11); He allows it to flow, but only to the limits that He set for it.

1.21.10.en: As for us, if God allows Satan to attack us, but within limits, we conquer by his attack if we are vigilant and thankful, so that the war becomes victory and triumph; and if we are slack and neglectful, Satan is not the cause of our harm; we are the cause. As St. John Chrysostom says: [Someone may say: Did not Adam get hurt, as his being was corrupted and he lost Paradise? No; the cause of this was the negligence of the one harmed, and his lack of self-control and striving. For Satan, who used various strong schemes, was unable to subdue Job; how then could he by a lesser means master Adam?!]

1.22.0.en: At the very time when the prophet declares his assurance that God, his holy and everlasting God, will not allow the people to die, but uses the Chaldeans for chastisement, he returns to reproach: "Thou art of purer eyes than to behold evil, and canst not look on iniquity: wherefore lookest thou upon the plunderers, and holdest thy peace when the wicked devoureth the man that is more righteous than he?!" [13].

1.22.1.en: The prophet Habakkuk knows what David the psalmist said: "For thou art not a God that hath pleasure in wickedness: neither shall evil dwell with thee" (Ps 5:4), and he understands what Jeremiah understood, that God hates the abominable thing (Jer 44:4), but he was perplexed how He could keep silent before what the wicked Chaldeans were doing to His people and look on the injustice, for the wicked had swallowed up one more righteous than himself. Here he does not say he swallowed up "the righteous," because the people were wicked, but compared with the Chaldeans they are more righteous than they.

1.22.2.en: Perhaps the word "look" or "behold" here does not mean mere seeing, for God knows all things, and nothing is hidden from Him; He has no need to look in order to see; rather, he means by it that He is pleased with their conduct and prospers their ways. For God's looking upon us means His caring for us and prospering our way.

1.22.3.en: The prophet began to bring out the traits of these wicked Chaldeans, whose way the Lord prospered for a time:

1.22.4.en: "And makest men as the fishes of the sea, as the creeping things, that have no ruler over them. They take up all of them with the angle, they catch them in their net, and gather them in their drag.

1.22.5.en: Therefore they rejoice and are glad.

1.22.6.en: Therefore they sacrifice unto their net, and burn incense unto their drag; because by them their portion is fat, and their meat plenteous (of the choicest - the Septuagint translation)

1.23.0.en: Shall they therefore empty their net, and not spare continually to slay the nations?" [14-17].

1.23.1.en: They looked at the other peoples as fish in the sea without an owner, with the right to catch what they please to eat and be satisfied, and as creeping things without authority, without price, to do with them what they wish. They rejoice and are glad when the hook brings up a fish or their nets gather many and men fall into their trap... They rejoice in human catches, offering idolatrous sacrifices and incense to their gods who grant them this precious catch. As though the prophet says to the Lord: Do You accept that Your people be fish without price in idolatrous nets, devoured by the wicked who offer sacrifices of thanks to the idols and incense before the idols?! Your people, in spite of what they have reached of deviation, are precious in Your eyes, so how can You leave them as prey for these Chaldeans?!

1.23.2.en: The nation of the Chaldeans rejoices in catching this people more than in catching any other people, for the prophet says: "because by them (by the angle and the net) their portion is fat, and their meat plenteous," or as it reads in the Septuagint, "their food is of the choicest," for it rejoices only in the choice catch. So the devil aims his arrows more at the best believers to draw them away from their faith, and as St. Jerome says: [Satan does not care for unbelievers, for they are outside... he wants only to corrupt the Church of Christ]

1.23.3.en: The wonder is that the enemy, the devil, like the Chaldeans, the fatter his portion becomes the more his greed increases and his heart is inflamed all the more to hunt others, for it is said: "Shall they therefore empty their net, and not spare continually to slay the nations?"
